name: Sam Rahman

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. We don't sell or campaign for anything. Your answers are confidential. What is an ordinary workday like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I fit handrails and replace damaged door jambs at the Market Baths renovation. I'm fifty-eight, trade certified and have spent enough years on sites to set an ordinary rail, though the curved stair still makes me slow down. My partner Leah cleans offices on short shifts, and our children are grown. The builder pays below the usual site rate, we have about twenty days of expenses saved, and there are only two other builders I could reach without a long commute. I occasionally use a phone AI tool to explain a plan mark, then check it with the site drawing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew a small improvement in the office forms is welcome if the baths doors still arrive when promised. I would keep fitting rails and look at what the tool actually gets right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I am already counting paydays. Leah's cleaning hours vary, and twenty days saved would not cover a long gap if the baths contract pauses for an ordinary reason.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep taking paid handrail shifts and check the next delivery date with site lead Tessa. In the first year I'd keep using the phone tool only for plan marks Tessa has verified, and phone the two other builders if the renovation loses a full week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about our own thin account, even though the AI part sounds mild. A late delivery would still mean a short pay packet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When was the phone explanation useful?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It explained a symbol for a fire-rated door, and Tessa confirmed the meaning before I drilled. I have used it since, but I would not let a phone tool choose a fixing on its own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a lost week force you to change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We would put off replacing the leaking kitchen tap and stop buying lunch near the site. Rent and Leah's travel fare have to be paid first.

I'd judge the tool by **real deliveries** and fitted rails.
think: Our **twenty-day cushion** is weak even without AI disruption.
Leah's **variable cleaning hours** cannot cover a long site gap.
do: Keep fitting **paid handrails** and check delivery dates with Tessa.
Use **verified phone notes** and contact local builders after a lost week.
feel: **Uneasy** about thin savings and possible delivery delays.
S0.quote: I would not let a phone tool choose a fixing on its own.
fieldNote: Sam's occasional AI use is limited to **verified plan symbols**, not choosing materials or safety fixings.
A **leaking tap** postponed after a lost week shows how little room the household already has.

steps.text: Keep taking paid handrail shifts at Market Baths
Use AI plan explanations only after Tessa verifies them
Contact two local builders if the renovation loses a week

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say stronger planning software could reduce late deliveries, but the crew should see an order tested on a real door. I would ask Tessa for the next phase dates before relying on a screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The office may be able to do estimates with fewer people, and the work reaching our site might come in starts and stops. I can learn a proven tool, but there are few paid rail jobs nearby if our own rota shrinks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll watch the buyer run one door order and compare its parts with the crate when it arrives. During the first year I'll keep paid baths shifts, and if the next phase has no start date I'll apply to both local builders and cut the bought lunches.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel interested in fewer wrong orders and anxious about the empty days they might hide. Our account cannot pay for a long trial with my wages missing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you look for in the crate?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The right hinges, the fire rating and the delivery day; all three matter before we fit a door. If the test works twice, I would learn the ordering screen on paid time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why not apply to a distant builder right away?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The bus fare and travel time would eat into this low wage. I would consider a real offer with higher pay, but not move my working day for a rumour.

I'd seek a **next-phase date** instead of relying on a screen.
think: The office change could bring **stop-start site work**.
Few **local rail jobs** make a reduced rota costly for us.
do: Watch **two real orders** and learn the screen if both work.
Keep **paid baths shifts** and apply locally if the next phase is undated.
Stop **bought lunches** if site hours fall.
feel: **Interested in fewer errors**, anxious about lost paid days.
S1.quote: Our account cannot pay for a long trial with my wages missing.
fieldNote: Sam's adoption test asks for **two complete orders** before learning the screen on paid time.
He rejects a speculative commute because **travel cost** would absorb too much of his low wage.

steps.text: Learn the ordering screen after two real door orders succeed

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the 2028 thinking system could take buying and plans, while site robots able to fit doors come around 2031. I would want a clear safety trial before my hands work next to one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll be sixty when office tasks change and sixty-three when robots may do my handrail and jamb work. Twenty days saved is almost no protection if I lose this wage, and Leah's cleaning shifts would not cover rent alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'll ask Tessa for the job dates and add a little to savings after full months when possible. In 2029 I'd take paid rail work while offered, apply to the two local repair crews if shifts fall, and ask the training centre about a funded building-maintenance placement; I'd enrol only if it pays a real wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about losing paid work by sixty-three, but I can still check offers and act. A course that has no wage would only make our short account shorter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a safe trial show?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A person must be able to stop the robot, and the rail must pass a load check before anyone leans on it. I would want the test on an actual awkward stair.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Leah tonight?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my partner Leah that we need the dates and the paid placement terms in writing. I won't call twenty days of savings a retirement plan.

say: I'd separate **2028 office work** from 2031 site robots.
I'd require an **awkward-stair safety trial** before working beside one.
think: At **sixty-three**, robots could take my paid rail fitting.
Our **twenty-day reserve** and Leah's shifts cannot cover rent without my wage.
do: Get **job dates** and save a little after full months.
Keep **paid rail work** in 2029 and apply if shifts fall.
Enrol in **maintenance training** only with a paid placement.
feel: **Anxious**, while still able to check real offers and act.
S2.quote: I won't call twenty days of savings a retirement plan.
fieldNote: Sam's **rent calculation** makes robot job loss serious despite his mid-level skill.
He will consider maintenance only through a **paid placement**, while keeping current paid site work.

steps.text: Keep taking paid rail shifts in 2029
Apply to two local repair crews if site hours fall
Enrol in maintenance training only if the placement pays a real wage
Set aside money after full paid months when possible

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years gives builders time to show workers the machines and the wages attached to any new role. I would ask for a calendar that covers both the office software and the later site robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At sixty-three thinking AI may change the orders, and at sixty-six robots may fit rails. I might want to work less then, but low pay and missed days mean I cannot tell Leah we'll have the money to stop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep taking baths jobs and ask Tessa for a rolling work calendar. In 2032 I'd still fit rails if paid work exists; if the calendar has a gap, I'll apply to the local repair crews, and after a full month I'd try to add a little to the savings tin.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel less rushed about the machines, but the next set of bills is unchanged. Five years can help only if enough of those weeks are paid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make a new role worth considering?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A stated wage, hours I can reach by bus and a safe way to do the work. I would not resign from rail fitting for an undefined post.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use the ordering software then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If two real orders came right and someone showed me the screen on paid time, yes. I pick up a tool once I can see it works on our site.

say: I'd seek a **combined work calendar** for office and site changes.
I'd ask for **wages attached** to any new role.
think: At **sixty-six**, robots may arrive before I can afford fewer hours.
Low pay and **missed days** undermine a long lead-in.
do: Keep **paid baths work** and request a rolling calendar.
Fit **rails in 2032** while paid shifts exist.
Apply locally after a gap and save a little after **full months**.
feel: Less **rushed by machines**, still worried about current bills.
S3.quote: Five years can help only if enough of those weeks are paid.
fieldNote: Sam makes the **five-year window** depend on real wages rather than a guessed retirement date.
His willingness to learn software remains tied to **proven orders** and instruction during paid hours.

steps.text: Keep taking paid rail-fitting shifts in 2032
Apply to local repair crews if the work calendar has a gap

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade allows time for a sensible safety rule before robots work around people. I would still ask the foreman when the next paid bath job starts, because that is the question for this winter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll be sixty-eight when thinking AI arrives and seventy-one when robots can fit rails. I may still need paid repairs then; our twenty-day cushion today gives me no honest retirement date to offer Leah.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep taking paid rail work, ask about the next local site and use checked plan notes only when helpful. In 2037 I'd take lighter paid repairs if my back allows and sit with Leah to compare actual wages, bills and savings before leaving work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about the distant robot date and anxious about next month's shift board. The horizon gives time, but it doesn't fill the savings tin today.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your children support you then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They have their own households, and I'd rather have them visit than pay our rent. We have to work from our own income first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would help this winter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A reliable run of paid bath repairs would let us clear the kitchen tap bill and start saving again. I do not need a prediction; I need a date and a wage.

I'd keep asking for the **next paid start** this winter.
think: At **sixty-eight**, I may still need paid rail repairs.
At **seventy-one**, our thin cushion gives no assured retirement date.
do: Keep **paid rail work** and checked plan notes.
Take **lighter repairs** in 2037 if wages are needed.
Count **bills and savings** with Leah before leaving work.
feel: **Anxious about current shifts**, calm about distant machines.
S4.quote: I do not need a prediction; I need a date and a wage.
fieldNote: The **distant robot date** does not ease Sam's immediate need for paid shifts and a repaired kitchen tap.
He would continue **paid repairs** at sixty-eight if needed and excludes adult children from the budget.

steps.text: Keep taking paid bath repair shifts while fit
Use AI plan explanations only after checking the drawing

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 picture worries me most because site robots could reach my rail work by sixty-three while we have only twenty days saved. A reliable calendar, safe trial and real paid repair openings would help me stay ahead of a cut.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask what happens when a delivery arrives late on a day I was ready to fit it. A late delivery costs me a day's wage even when nobody calls the order wrong.

headlineQuote: A late delivery costs me a day's wage even when nobody calls the order wrong.
portrait: Sam is a **fifty-eight-year-old certified** carpenter with mid-level skill on bath repairs.
His low site rate, Leah's variable cleaning shifts and **twenty days saved** keep wage gaps close.
He uses AI **now and then**, only after checking plan notes with a site lead.
He looks for **paid local work** and tests new ordering tools against actual deliveries.
biggestWorry: The **2028 path** could remove his rail-fitting wage around 2031 with little savings.
whatWouldHelp: He wants a **reliable calendar**, safe trials and paid local repair openings.
